articles.body:
Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters on Tuesday said the GOP is “going to defy history to” maintain control of Congress after the midterms.

Gruters told NewsNation host Blake Burman on “The Hill” that Republicans have better candidates, more resources and “a financial advantage” to “win these seats.”

“Get ready because we’re going state by state, district to district, and we’re going to make sure we push our candidates over the victory line, and we’re going to defy history to win this November,” he added.

When the president’s party controls Congress going into the midterms, the opposing party typically claims the majority as a referendum on the president. Republicans and President Trump, however, hope to keep GOP control and pass his legislative agenda.

Gruters noted the GOP has the “best showman that’s ever existed” in Trump, who will “anchor” both nights of the first-ever RNC midterm convention , which kicks off Wednesday afternoon in Dallas. The RNC chair has been among those promoting the event, describing it as a “ Trump-a-palooza ,” with dozens of administration officials set to speak, including Vice President Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

“This is our way to get our message directly to the American people about all the great things that this administration has done and all the things that we want to continue to do,” Gruters added.

The nonpartisan election analyst Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) earlier this week shifted its November forecast for the Senate to “ a pure toss-up ” for the first time since early June. DDHQ predicts Democrats will retake control of the House, pegging the likelihood of the outcome at 67 percent as of Tuesday.

Some Republicans feel mixed about the event , citing concerns about the cost, timing and potential political risk of being so closely associated with Trump just less than eight weeks from the midterms.

Some former GOP lawmakers have said the focus on the president and his actions, including posting online about renaming geographical locations such as Lake Ontario and New Mexico , could hurt Republican chances of maintaining control of Congress.

“I mean, all these sorts of things that are completely irrelevant to Americans’ lives and, frankly, they think it’s bizarre, just renaming states and lakes and the Gulf,” former Rep. Charlie Dent (R-Pa.) told MS NOW on Monday, referring to the Gulf of Mexico.

He continued, “So again, a distraction, but these are not helping the president or his party.”

articles.title: Why conservatives have shifted on Israel
articles.summary: The political formation of young conservatives is increasingly happening on the internet.
articles.body:
After investing $32 million into Michigan’s Democratic primary, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, known as AIPAC, planned on spending heavily to defeat progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed in the general election. To AIPAC’s surprise, Republican nominee Mike Rogers turned down its offer.

While the Trump administration continues to tout its pro-Israel line, the rest of the party is starting to shift. The conservative turn on Israel has been years in the making. What was once an unimpeachable consensus on the right has fractured under pressure from a new generation of internet-savvy conservatives.

I went through millions of online comments to document this shift. The generational gap within the conservative coalition is hard to overstate.

According to a recent New York Times/Siena poll , 72 percent of Republicans under 30 believe President Trump has been too supportive of Israel. Only 11 percent of conservatives over age 65 agree.

Even among evangelicals — historically the most reliably pro-Israel demographic — less than one-third of young people favor Israel over the Palestinians. This generational shift has been on open display since the start of the Iran War; a conflict younger Republicans are only half as likely to support as their older peers.

The political formation of young conservatives is increasingly happening on the internet. Many young Republicans gravitate toward controversial figures such as Tucker Carlson or Steve Bannon, who have challenged the traditional consensus on Israel. A noteworthy share of Republican staffers in Washington follow white nationalist streamer Nick Fuentes — the political director of the College Republicans of America is an avowed fan. Meanwhile, Ben Shapiro, staunchly pro-Israel and once a darling of young conservatives nationwide, had seen a huge drop in YouTube viewership as of earlier this summer.

But the recent internet wars on the right are a symptom rather than the cause of the conservative turn on Israel. My analysis of one of the internet’s largest conservative chat groups — Reddit’s r/conservative subreddit — found that negative comments averaged around 40 percent of Israel-related posts even prior to October 2023.

Carlson and Candace Owens, popular podcasters of the online right, turned against Israel long before the first U.S.-Israel-Iran war. The shift at the party base, in other words, precedes the recent backlash over Israel’s alleged hand in Trump’s war on Iran.

The reasons range from the eschatological to the political. Among young evangelicals, support for Israel plummeted from 75 to 33 percent between 2018 and 2021 and has stayed remarkably stable since. This has much to do with a change in theology. Whereas Christian Zionists traditionally believe that Jewish control of the Holy Land is a sign of the Second Coming, younger pastors have largely moved away from such millenarian prophecies. My clustering algorithm showed less than five percent of conservative commenters focus on religious ties.

Antisemitism seems to play a role as well. A Yale poll found that two-thirds of self-described “extreme conservatives” held antisemitic views. Jew-hating “Groyper” trolls dominate many of the darkest corners of the internet, giving a resurgence to old antisemitic ideas. And news of mounting anti-Christian attacks in Israel have revived age-old conspiracies of a perpetual war between Jews and Christians.

Still, the conservative shift is not merely a reflection of domestic politics. Young Americans have come of age amid a succession of right-wing Israeli governments that openly reject a two-state solution and have done little to refute accusations of widespread discrimination and apartheid . Fewer than one in 10 young Americans back Israel’s actions in Gaza — a remarkable consensus for an age group uniquely polarized along gender and party lines.

For a generation tired of foreign engagements , America’s special relationship with Israel feels much like an anachronism. Among the Redditors in our dataset, concerns over Israel’s political influence played a role as well — a fear only heightened by Netanyahu’s role in the war in Iran.

So far, the MAGA establishment, hesitant to buck Trump’s lead, has been slow to respond to these concerns. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), a Trump critic who is not seeking reelection, was a lone Republican vote in favor of an amendment blocking military assistance to Israel. Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, whose campaign mixed anti-Israel sentiment with nativist rhetoric, finished a distant third in his state’s Republican primary. As with immigration and trade a decade ago, Republican elites today lag far behind the younger party base when it comes to the issue of Israel.

There are signs that Republican leadership is catching up. JD Vance, widely seen as the Republican frontrunner for 2028, has already made not-so-subtle hints that there is daylight between himself and Trump on Israel. Meanwhile, AIPAC backing is increasingly becoming a liability on the right as well.

Trump has reportedly worried out loud that he will be the last pro-Israel U.S. president. Many young conservatives are hoping he is right.

Johannes Lang is an AI researcher and McCain Global Leader focusing on the domestic politics of U.S. foreign policy.

articles.title: O’Reilly: Republicans ‘still running in the old model’
articles.summary: Political commentator Bill O’Reilly said Tuesday that Republicans have not updated their framework to efficiently fight against the current iteration of the Democratic Party. “But the movement that the Democratic Party represents to the far, far left, that’s new. And, the Republicans have not really seized upon it yet,” O’Reilly said during an appearance on…
articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly said Tuesday that Republicans have not updated their framework to efficiently fight against the current iteration of the Democratic Party.

“But the movement that the Democratic Party represents to the far, far left, that’s new. And, the Republicans have not really seized upon it yet,” O’Reilly said during an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance.”

“They’re still running in the old model of, ‘Vote for me and I’ll set you free,’ OK? And it’s names on a ballot,” he told host Leland Vittert. “It’s not what’s happening here. People have to decide what kind of country they want to live in. Do you want to live in a country run by Democrats who are going to continue taxation forever?”

In the last few months, progressive insurgent candidates, including democratic socialists , have locked down victories in Democratic primaries in places ranging from Michigan to Colorado, defeating more establishment candidates.

More moderate figures in the party, like Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.), have pushed back against rising momentum on the left, as a growing rift within the caucus comes into view.

And some progressives have seen their stars rise in the last few years, with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) now one of the most prominent faces in the party after winning his election last year and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) being discussed as a potential 2028 presidential candidate .

In a poll released last month, Democrats had a more favorable view of socialism versus capitalism , with more than half of respondents in the party seeing the ideology in a “very positive” or “somewhat positive” light.

articles.title: Obama judge's peculiar Trump rebuke ignites fury over 'unprofessional' language: 'Embarrassment'
articles.summary: Three Obama-appointed judges blocked the IRS from sharing taxpayer addresses with ICE on Tuesday, with one calling the argument "weak sauce."
articles.body: Critics took aim Tuesday at a federal appeals court after a judge dismissed the IRS’ argument in an ICE data-sharing case as "weak sauce," drawing immediate backlash over the unusual language in the ruling. "That argument is ‘weak sauce’ where the district court has permitted the IRS to file any necessary notifications ‘under seal,’ thereby shielding any criminal investigative activity from disclosure," wrote D.C. Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama in 2013. "Weak sauce" is slang for something that falls flat and lacks substance. The lawsuit centers on whether the IRS violated federal tax-confidentiality law by sharing tens of thousands of taxpayer addresses with ICE after receiving requests for information on more than 1 million suspected illegal immigrants. The case was heard by a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel composed entirely of Obama appointees: Pillard, Patricia Millett and Robert Wilkins. OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORCHES TRUMP ADMIN IN LATEST COURTROOM SHOWDOWN, REFERS ATTORNEY FOR BAR REVIEW Critics were quick to slam Pillard’s "weak sauce" comment, calling it an "embarrassment" while others slammed the ruling. "DHS strongly disagrees with this ruling. We will continue using every lawful tool available to locate and remove illegal aliens with final orders of removal, and this ruling in no way prevents us from doing so," DHS told Fox News Digital on Wednesday. "It's an embarrassment to the Court that 2 judges would not have told the author to change a different phrase with the same meaning. Now that is going to be quoted/cited in future cases and it will look sophomoric and unserious," said conservative attorney William Shipley on X. "Three anti-Trump Obama judges abuse power to impair basic immigration law enforcement. We have a judicial integrity crisis in the federal courts," wrote Judicial Watch president Tom Fitton. "Why would anyone put that language in a professional document of any kind? That goes beyond legal decorum. It’s just unprofessional across the board," said one user on X. "I’m all for using accessible language, but the insertion of popular slang in judicial opinions is getting out of hand," another posted to X. "Make legal writing formal again," wrote D.C. attorney Joshua Prince. GOP SENATOR UNVEILS BOASBERG ACT TO STOP 'ROGUE' JUDGES FROM HANDPICKING TRUMP CASES "Did Ketanji write that or some TikTok fan girl? Borderline illiteracy," said one user. The plaintiffs—including the Center for Taxpayer Rights, Main Street Alliance and two labor unions—argued the IRS failed to ensure ICE’s requests met strict legal requirements. APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS The judges upheld a lower-court order blocking the IRS from using its current process to provide taxpayer information to ICE, finding that the procedure failed to comply with federal tax-confidentiality law. The judges found that ICE often submitted "either incomplete or insufficiently populated" information, yet the IRS still provided tens of thousands of taxpayer addresses. The ruling comes as President Donald Trump has made immigration enforcement a central priority, directing the administration to expand border security, detention and deportations while ICE ramps up arrests nationwide. articles.title: Watchdog reviewing whistleblower’s mail-in voting rules warning
articles.summary: The U.S. Postal Service’s Office of Inspector General is reviewing a new system for handling mail-in ballots that could cause problems cause in the November midterms. The watchdog said Tuesday that it will independently examine allegations raised by a whistleblower about the agency’s computer system that could jeopardize mail-in voting. The whistleblower warned that USPS…
articles.body:
The U.S. Postal Service’s Office of Inspector General is reviewing a new system for handling mail-in ballots that could cause problems cause in the November midterms.

The watchdog said Tuesday that it will independently examine allegations raised by a whistleblower about the agency’s computer system that could jeopardize mail-in voting.

The whistleblower warned that USPS was rushing to develop an online portal to check information about voters receiving ballots by mail, and that the system was riddled with errors.

According to Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who publicized the allegations, the whistleblower claimed the project began around June 15 and was being developed in roughly three months, despite similar systems typically taking longer to build.

The whistleblower also alleged some testing was skipped and employees were unclear how the system was supposed to operate.

These problems , the whistleblower warned, could lead to eligible voters not receiving their ballots.

USPS has defended its work on the portal in a statement , saying it will ensure that mail-in ballots are received “securely, reliably and efficiently,” and that it is reviewing the concerns raised by Blumenthal and the whistleblower.

USPS Postmaster General David Steiner said that while the project was developed on an accelerated timeline, the agency’s “standards for quality, security, and system integrity were not compromised.”

“Testing and validation have been continuous throughout the development lifecycle, and our process requires that deployment be delayed whenever significant defects or security vulnerabilities are identified, until those issues are appropriately resolved,” Steiner said in a statement .

The new system is part of a broader Postal Service rule implementing an executive order President Trump signed in March.

Under the rule, states would have to provide USPS lists of voters receiving mail ballots, and USPS could refuse to send ballots that do not meet its requirements.

The rule was blocked by a judge from taking effect after U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the Trump administration and the Postal Service did not have the authority to impose the voting requirements.

articles.title: Newsom accuses Trump of lying during his 9/11 attack response anecdote
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Tuesday accused President Trump of lying after he told an anecdote about his actions in the days surrounding the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York City. Trump, during an event honoring 9/11 first responders at the White House, said he was carried away from One Liberty Plaza,…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Tuesday accused President Trump of lying after he told an anecdote about his actions in the days surrounding the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in New York City.

Trump, during an event honoring 9/11 first responders at the White House, said he was carried away from One Liberty Plaza, formerly called the U.S. Steel Building, which started to creak after the attack. The president said two firefighters grabbed his arms and “they literally lifted me up.”

“They lifted me up and they started running with me,” he continued. “I said, ‘Fellas, I can run myself.’ But they were amazing. But they thought it was coming down. It didn’t come down.”

Newsom shared journalist Aaron Rupar’s post on social platform X that characterized Trump’s account as though “he was basically lifted out of the rubble on 9/11.” The California Democrat commented, “An absolutely disgusting thing to lie about.”

New York Magazine also referred to his speech as a “ weird lie ,” though Trump responded and accused the magazine of claiming he was not at Ground Zero.

He defended the accuracy of his speech, writing on Truth Social that he was “obviously not” there on Sept. 11, when the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center collapsed, “but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction workers.”

The president, then a businessman inside Trump Tower on New York City’s Fifth Avenue, notably called in to WWOR-TV as the events of 9/11 unfolded and described his building as being the tallest in lower Manhattan after the towers fell.

But the earliest images of Trump near the area were filmed on Sept. 13, 2001, for two interviews that day . He said at the time that his company had more than 100 workers assisting with the recovery. But former New York Fire Department battalion chief Richard Alles told PolitiFact in 2019 that there would be a record of the president and the 100 or more workers at Ground Zero.

“Is there a chance he was ever down there by himself and I didn’t know it?” Alles told the fact-checker. “It’s possible, but I know of no one who ever witnessed him there.”

Former New York Police Commissioner Bernard Kerik told Breitbart News in 2019 that Trump came to the area “numerous times” to “motivate and inspire the men and women down there that were working on the pile.”

Trump is slated to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks with a speech at the Pentagon , one of the targets hijackers struck that day. The native New Yorker will not attend the commemoration in New York City, where the four surviving former presidents and Vice President Vance are scheduled to attend.

articles.title: Is David Beasley the most interesting second act in politics?
articles.summary: Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley, known for his principled stance on removing the Confederate flag and his leadership as UN World Food Programme head, launched the Breaking Bread Together movement to bridge American political and cultural divides.
articles.body:
Not many political figures I know find a measure of peace in losing an election on a matter of principle. Only one went on to accept a Nobel Prize and now dedicates himself to healing the great rift in American politics.

Meet former Republican South Carolina Gov. David Beasley.

Beasley flashed like a meteor on the American political scene in the 1980s and 1990s.

He was elected to the South Carolina House of Representatives in 1978 at age 20 as a Democrat and rose through the ranks: majority whip, majority leader, then the youngest speaker pro tempore in the nation . In 1991, he joined the great migration of Southern Democrats into the ranks of Reagan Republicans. He was elected governor in 1994, and almost immediately, his name began flapping from pundits’ lips as a future Republican presidential contender. He governed as a conventional conservative, supporting economic development, welfare reform and pro-business initiatives. He also focused on prison reform and improving educational standards.

Reelection seemed all but guaranteed; a future in national politics entirely plausible.

Then South Carolina endured a wave of racially motivated church arsons and firebombings by Ku Klux Klan members.

Until then, Beasley had opposed calls to move the Confederate flag from the state House dome. The hate crimes changed everything for him.

He prayed. He deliberated. He listened to Black church leaders describe the terror they felt in their own sanctuaries, and the trauma of seeing the same flag embraced by white supremacists flying above their state Capitol. I imagine he also did what any political leader would do in that epic clash between moral conscience and political efficacy: carefully weigh the electoral risks.

In November 1996, he announced in a statewide television address that he had changed his position. He wanted the flag removed from the Capitol dome and placed beside a Confederate soldier monument instead. It may have seemed a decent compromise. But it drew fierce backlash: Many on the left said it did not go far enough; many on the right called it a broken promise and a betrayal of their heritage.

It is almost possible to say with absolute certainty that his reversal cost him reelection in 1998. Any political textbook will tell you that when your base is dispirited and your opposition is energized, you are running uphill on a Blue Ridge mountain.

On the night of his defeat, Beasley called his senior staff together. There was no doubt that his position on the Confederate flag had influenced the outcome. His advisors had even urged him to hold on discussing the issue until he secured his “certain” second term. But while the election was close, Beasley held his values closer.

Upon gathering his disparate team, he posed three questions: Did we do what was right? Did we do it at the right time? And did we do it the right way? Not in judgment or the chaos of division, but out of love for our neighbors, and a desire to bring people together. His team answered yes on all fronts. By that measure, Beasley deemed the campaign a success.

Beasley was not new to the cause of civil rights. His parents had been active in the movement, and he grew up in a predominantly Black community. His past caught up with his future, and his political career was over.

After leaving office, Beasley received the John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award from U.S. Sen. Ted Kennedy (D-Mass.) for his effort to remove the flag. In February 2017, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley nominated him to become the next executive director of the World Food Programme . During his term, he immersed himself — literally — in famines, insurrections, pandemics, and civil wars around the world. In December 2020, Beasley accepted the Nobel Peace Prize on behalf of the WFP for its efforts to combat world hunger.

His term was scheduled to expire in 2022. But United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres extended it amid the food crises created by the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russo-Ukrainian War. President Biden initially opposed the extension, but bipartisan support in Congress helped change the administration’s position. Beasley’s term as executive director finally expired in April 2023.

What does one do after intervening in conflicts across the globe?

His third act arrived in August with the launch of Breaking Bread Together , a national movement designed to bridge political, cultural and religious divides across America through shared meals. His goal is to use faith not as cudgel, but as an invitation to conversation. To inspire us to listen more and pontificate less. His point is that real change starts around kitchen tables, church halls and on community farms, not inside the Beltway.

The man has heart, but do not underestimate his natural political skills. I saw them for myself when we first met at a Washington, D.C. cafe with a menu of mostly unpronounceable beverages. Our server was a Black woman who spoke with a slight accent. Beasley’s ears perked up, and he asked where she was from.

Beasley immediately switched to fluent French, asking about her life and establishing an instant connection.

I may not agree with every one of his positions. But I believe political discourse needs his approach, and the next generation of political leaders could learn from it: Leave room to change your mind. Listen carefully. You can stand on principle and even suffer politically for it, yet still make the world a better place …perhaps one meal at a time.

Steve Israel represented New York in the House of Representatives for eight terms and was chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee from 2011 to 2015.

images.caption: Former United Nations World Food Program Executive Director and Nobel Peace Prize winner David Beasley speaks to the South Carolina General Assembly on Wednesday, May 2, 2023 in Columbia, S.C. Beasley was governor of South Carolina from 1995 to 1999. (AP Photo/Jeffrey Collins)

articles.title: Missouri court opens contempt probe into Republican official over redistricting fight
articles.summary: The no-holds-barred fight over congressional maps in Missouri has reached a new level of intensity with the state’s high court opening a contempt probe into Secretary of State Denny Hoskins.
articles.body: The no-holds-barred fight over congressional maps in Missouri has reached a new level of intensity with the state’s high court opening a contempt probe into Secretary of State Denny Hoskins. The Missouri Supreme Court late Tuesday issued an order asking Hoskins, a Republican, to explain “why he should not be held in contempt” for violating a ruling last week that said the state cannot use a newly drawn GOP map. Despite the ruling, Hoskins continued to push to use the new map. The court also ordered Hoskins to appear in person when the judges hold a hearing in the case Thursday. Hoskins indicated in a post on X that he would not back down. “I look forward to my day in court,” he said. The state court order came after a flurry of court activity Tuesday. First, the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a last-ditch appeal from Hoskins seeking to use the new map, which seeks to eliminate a Democratic-held congressional seat in the state. Soon after, a federal judge in Missouri issued a new ruling saying the state is required to use the new map, setting up a dispute between federal and state courts. Litigation in that case continues and could soon reach the nation’s highest court again. The 2025 Republican redistricting plan, part of a wave of redistricting encouraged by President Donald Trump, sought to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. Should the Missouri Supreme Court ruling remain in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election. The Republican-led Legislature redrew the map for the November elections, seeking to eliminate one of those Democratic seats. The legal fight was kick-started when a group called People Not Politicians, led by activist Richard von Glahn, gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would veto the Legislature’s map and put it on hold for the 2026 election while people voted on it. But Hoskins refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to being overturned by voters. The Missouri Supreme Court, which has a majority of Republican appointees, disagreed, saying there was nothing in state law that exempted redistricting maps from being vetoed by voters via the referendum process. The state court’s contempt order came in response to a filing made by the referendum proponents’ lawyers.

articles.title: Trump gave Natalie Harp, other aides $45K gifts: Disclosures
articles.summary: President Trump gifted several White House aides — including longtime assistant Natalie Harp — $45,000 cash gifts, according to financial disclosures released by the Trump administration last week. The payments, which totaled $135,000, were marked as “Cash Gift for Holidays” and attributed to the president on the disclosure forms. Three of Trump’s closest aides —…
articles.body:
President Trump gifted several White House aides — including longtime assistant Natalie Harp — $45,000 cash gifts, according to financial disclosures released by the Trump administration last week.

The payments, which totaled $135,000, were marked as “Cash Gift for Holidays” and attributed to the president on the disclosure forms.

Three of Trump’s closest aides — Harp, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris, who each have an annual taxpayer-funded salary of $150,000 — received these gifts.

Harp serves as a special assistant and executive assistant to the president. The former conservative TV anchor has come under public scrutiny amid reports about her proximity and devotion to Trump.

Harris, the deputy director of Oval Office operations and an executive assistant to the president, was also nominated by Trump to the Commission of Fine Arts. The federal panel is responsible for reviewing architectural and design decisions around Washington, including the president’s controversial White House ballroom project .

Martin is Trump’s communications adviser, and she films social media content for the president at the White House and during his trips abroad.

Another White House employee, Oval Office Operations Director Walt Nauta, received a $20,000 gift from the president, according to a financial disclosure. Nauta has an annual salary of $175,000, according to public White House records.

The Washington Post first reported on the cash gifts.

Richard Painter, a White House ethics lawyer under former President George W. Bush and vocal Trump critic, pointed to a federal statute that bars federal employees from receiving supplemental funding. Both the person who pays and the person who receives this supplemental income are liable under federal law.

“A White House staffer is not your Fifth Avenue doorman,” Painter wrote on social platform X . “No tipping, and no holiday gifts from a current boss or former employer. The salary is what it is. Full stop.”

A White House spokesperson pushed back against accusations that these gifts violated any rules in a statement shared with The Hill.

“The President has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector,” the spokesperson said.

“The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards,” they added.

articles.title: White House removes ‘Build the Wall’ game from website after Tetris posts warning
articles.summary: The White House removed MAGA-themed game “Build the Wall” from its website this week after the Tetris Co.
articles.body: The White House removed MAGA-themed game “Build the Wall” from its website this week after the Tetris Co. issued a statement online alluding to copyright infringement. Last week, the White House unveiled a series of video games centered on President Donald Trump’s agenda, which mirrored popular games such as “Tetris,” “Snake” and “Flappy Bird.” The “Tetris”-like game had players stack “bricks” to build the wall along the southern border. The game introduction instructed users to “hold the line” against a “zombie border siege.” Tetris quickly pushed back, saying in a post on X that it “was not involved in the creation” of the game and takes “copyright infringement very seriously.” “At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” the company said last week in an online statement. “To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we’re grateful to have you in our community.” An internet archival version of the White House website, saved by the Wayback Machine, indicates that the game was still on the site as of Monday afternoon, but disappeared Tuesday. The White House did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the game’s removal. Tetris Co. declined to comment. The other games, which still appear on the White House’s website, also mirror popular existing games. A game titled “Rio Run,” for example, instructs players to “patrol the line along the river” and “pick up every crosser.” It resembles the popular game “Snake.” Another game, “Flappy Bill,” resembles the game “Flappy Bird,” and instructs players controlling a bald eagle to “keep the bill in the air while flying through monuments.” The White House also posted videos that mimicked content from popular video game companies in order to promote the new slate of games. In one video it posted last week, the White House promoted the arcade website using a modified version of the Xbox startup animation. In another promotional video, the White House modified the “Sega” startup animation and sound, changing it to “MAGA.” The White House also posted a promotional video directly mimicking the Nintendo GameCube startup. On Tuesday, the White House also released a video on its X account mirroring the Nintendo game “The Legend of Zelda.” The introduction screen read “The Legend of Trump” and “Make America Great Again,” featuring the Nintendo game’s logo and font. The video also uses a song from the game. Nintendo, Sega and Xbox did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the White House’s arcade. The White House has previously released political content that used material directly invoking or altering popular video games and fictional characters from books and animated series. The Trump administration has often used copyrighted songs in the background of political videos, sometimes prompting artists to publicly disavow the White House’s use of their music. In December, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posted an image depicting the children’s book character Franklin the Turtle in combat gear, firing a bazooka at small, package-laden boats from a helicopter along with the words, “Franklin Targets Narco Terrorists” and “A Classic Franklin Story.” The publishing house, Kids Can Press, condemned the use of the character, saying in a post on X that it strongly condemns “any denigrating, violent, or unauthorized use of Franklin’s name or image.” That same month, musician Sabrina Carpenter blasted the White House for using one of her songs in a video showing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers detaining people. She called the video “evil and disgusting” and added, “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

articles.title: Lengthy deployments like the USS Lincoln’s hurt military mental health
articles.summary: Members of the military aren’t invincible.
articles.body:
The USS Abraham Lincoln left San Diego last November for what was supposed to be a six-month deployment . Instead, the carrier went to sea for more than 250 days and was on pace for the second-longest deployment on record since the Vietnam War.

The title for the longest modern-era carrier deployment is held by the USS Gerald R. Ford, which spent 326 days at sea — a record set back in May.

The increasing frequency of these long missions raises a serious question: Is the U.S. government doing enough to support the brave men and women aboard these ships as they work tirelessly to protect America’s national security?

Those who have endured long deployments know firsthand the toll these prolonged missions can have on service members’ mental state. The USS Lincoln’s extended time away “can lead to serious mental health issues during deployment, upon return from it, or after completion of military service,” says John Stewart , a retired Air Force chief master sergeant.

Reports of poor conditions aboard these carriers are troubling. Last spring, during the USS Ford’s 10th month of deployment, a fire broke out on board that displaced 600 sailors from their beds. Many were forced to sleep on floors and tables throughout the ship.

According to family accounts of those aboard the USS Lincoln, reports of food shortages, a lack of supplies and broken plumbing have caused a worrisome drop in sailor morale. Worse, multiple sailors have reportedly tried to jump overboard from the USS Lincoln. This must be taken seriously, as facts show suicide is the number one cause of death among active-duty American military personnel.

These disturbing allegations demand a thorough investigation — which some members of Congress have requested . Yet it is unclear whether any inquiry will happen. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has brushed aside claims about the deteriorating conditions aboard the USS Lincoln, saying they have been “completely misrepresented.”

President Trump, when asked about the extended length of the USS Lincoln’s mission, said the ship’s time at sea “ was not nearly long enough ,” suggesting future carrier deployments could be as long — or potentially longer — than the beleaguered ship’s recent assignment.

And the Pentagon chose to terminate the publisher and top editor at Stars and Stripes, the military publication that broke the story about the strenuous environment aboard the USS Lincoln.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) wrote to Secretary Hegseth, saying the Pentagon “owes” the sailors “not only adequate supplies, maintenance, and support during this deployment, but a sustainable force-generation model that does not rely on repeatedly extending sailors and ships to meet persistent operational demands.”

Other questions remain as to what the Pentagon is doing to proactively address the mental health of those impacted by these long carrier missions. The U.S. Navy and broader Armed Forces have worked to destigmatize mental health and encourage military members to seek help if they need it. But a deeply rooted cultural perception remains, and many of those in uniform still feel compelled to internalize their own personal struggles.

Toughing-it-out is the military mentality, and seeking help is often misperceived as a sign of weakness. A recent study found nearly 60 percent of veterans and military personnel who would otherwise benefit from mental health support avoid seeking treatment for fear of being judged or seen as unfit for service, among other factors. That misguided sentiment can discourage people from acknowledging problems until it’s too late. We must dismantle this outdated mindset.

Members of the military aren’t invincible. They’re not incapable of feeling the effects of stress, loneliness or exhaustion. And when these challenges are too difficult for them to bear, the Pentagon must establish a culture where consulting professional help is considered an act of valor, not a lack of strength.

Lengthy deployments are sometimes unavoidable. Military operations are fluid, and situations arise that often require soldiers to persevere through difficult circumstances. But when they occur, America’s service members must have confidence that they will have access to essentials — food, water, hygiene products and functional plumbing — so that they can perform their duties to the best of their abilities.

Hegseth’s refusal to even acknowledge the taxing conditions aboard the USS Lincoln is a failure in leadership. It also stands in stark contrast to what he has told recruits and their families, where he has promised that he would “have their back.”

We owe a massive debt to the men and women who proudly defend our country. Having their back requires more than pledging commitment and expressing thanks for their service.

It demands our elected leaders have the courage to acknowledge when we have made mistakes, the conviction to put corrective measures in place so we don’t repeat them and the fortitude to provide soldiers the care and supplies they need to do their job effectively.

America’s service members deserve nothing less.

Lyndon Haviland, DrPH, MPH, is a distinguished scholar at the CUNY School of Public Health and Health Policy.

articles.title: Armed man accused of lunging at Ohio Dem candidate avoids felonies as prosecutor reveals key evidence
articles.summary: Patrick Havas' own video is the only footage of the Canfield Fair incident after Amy Acton's camp allegedly asked people to stop recording it.
articles.body: The man who allegedly stormed toward Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton at a recent fair will not face felony charges, the county prosecutor leading the case told reporters Tuesday. The only video investigators currently have of the incident was recorded by the suspect, Patrick Havas, leaving authorities with little video evidence, Mahoning County Prosecutor Lynn Maro said. "The information we've received is that the Acton camp requested individuals stop recording shortly before this incident occurred," Maro told reporters on Tuesday. "So, at this point, the only video we have is the defendant’s. And what's that showing certainly doesn't support filing felony charges." PISTOL-PACKING MAN KNOCKS OVER FAIRGOERS FORCING HIS WAY TOWARD OHIO GOVERNOR CANDIDATE AMY ACTON, POLICE SAY Patrick Havas was intercepted by Ohio Highway Patrol officers after allegedly knocking over multiple fairgoers as he ran toward Acton at a tent at the Canfield Fair while armed with a Taser and two firearms. He was initially booked on two counts of assault and one count of disorderly conduct, all misdemeanors. An inducing panic charge was added Tuesday at his arraignment, bringing the total to four misdemeanor counts. Havas pleaded not guilty. Campaigns have often prohibited or advised against filming candidates to prevent "trackers," or opposition research individuals with cameras, from filming the interactions to look for a politically weak spot to focus on. Then-candidate Bernie Moreno employed audio-jamming technology in 2024, with his campaign acknowledging such to Business Insider. The campaign told the outlet the jammer was only used against trackers and not voters. When asked by an NPR reporter about online conjecture that the Acton team "overblew" the incident, DeWine reportedly replied the idea is "total garbage. "No one overblew it. Facts are facts. These are not good situations, and they’re anti-democratic," DeWine said, according to the report. Maro said the tape showed Havas "walking into the tent" where Acton was, and "calling out her name" before executive protection unit officers from Ohio Highway Patrol interrupted him. "Then, his phone is either dropped or tossed, and that’s all we have," Maro said. RAMASWAMY TORCHES DEM RIVAL OVER 'OUTRAGEOUS' COVID-19 CLAIM: 'SPEWING LIES' "There's never any close contact with the governor, never gets near her — sorry, ‘candidate for governor’," she added. Fox News Digital reached out to Maro for comment and to obtain a copy of the video in question. An official who picked up the phone at her office said Maro was out but would be checking messages. A reporter for the NBC affiliate tweeted that their network had also attempted to obtain the video but that officials said they would not be releasing it as part of their "active investigation." Fox News Digital also reached out to the Acton campaign for additional comment, as well as details around the reported request that people stop filming Acton just before the encounter. "While attending the Canfield Fair, an armed individual lunged at Dr. Acton, injuring multiple people. Dr. Acton and Eric are grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured," Acton campaign communications director Addie Bullock said in a separate statement. "This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another." An Ohio judge ordered Havas to not speak to the press, according to Youngstown’s NBC affiliate, and Havas has been placed under a $5,000 bond and forced to surrender any weaponry in his possession. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Havas is a local to that region of Ohio. He was arrested in 2008 on petty theft and disorderly conduct charges, according to Newsweek. The theft charge was later dismissed after he pleaded no contest to disorderly conduct. He was accused of stealing several movies from a supermarket, including the James Bond film "Casino Royale." DeWine’s lieutenant, former Ohio State Football coach Jim Tressel, declined to run for the office. Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

articles.title: $54M CodePink-linked foundation shut down in California pops up at ramshackle Miami home
articles.summary: Arc of Justice, led by CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin, lost its California registration and resurfaced as a Florida nonprofit at a Miami duplex.
articles.body: A far-left foundation that bankrolled CodePink and recently reported $54.6 million in assets before being shut down by California regulators has resurfaced at a ramshackle Miami home. Arc of Justice, led by CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin, lost its charitable registration after years of failing to file required financial paperwork with California. But what appears to be the same nonprofit is now registered at a small, single-story house owned by Benjamin's longtime partner and fellow activist, Tighe Barry, documents viewed by Fox News Digital show. The sequence of events raises questions about why it fell out of compliance in California. HOUSE PANEL SUBPOENAS 3 LEFT-WING GROUPS IN PROBE OF $39M TIED TO MARXIST TYCOON NEVILLE SINGHAM Arc of Justice has poured millions of dollars into left-wing and progressive activist organizations over the years, including CodePink, Global Exchange, the Alliance for Global Justice and the National Iranian American Council, according to IRS filings. Federal tax returns provided to Fox News Digital by Arc of Justice's attorney show the California foundation's assets grew from $51.4 million at the end of 2023 to $54.6 million at the end of 2024, while it continued distributing millions of dollars in grants. CodePink has campaigned against U.S. policy toward China and Cuba and has been accused by congressional investigators of promoting Chinese Communist Party interests — allegations the group has denied. Benjamin, who has been a political activist for decades and has often disrupted congressional hearings, co-founded CodePink with Jodie Evans, the wife of Shanghai-based Marxist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham, whose funding network has come under congressional and federal scrutiny over alleged foreign influence and the use of tax-exempt organizations. Now it’s Arc of Justice’s finances that are coming under the microscope. "It's pretty unusual. Most private foundations are fairly scrupulous on their compliance efforts," Patrick Sternal, a former IRS official who specialized in tax-exempt organizations, told Fox News Digital. "So it's unusual for a private foundation with that much in the bank to fall out of compliance and to be suspended." Registration revoked in California The California Attorney General's Office, led by Democrat Rob Bonta, revoked Arc of Justice's charitable registration in January 2025 after it failed to submit required annual filings with the state for 2020 through 2024. The foundation had already been suspended for more than a year before the revocation. The state Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital that Arc of Justice had continually failed to respond to the registry's delinquency and suspension notices before its registration was revoked. Under the revocation, Arc of Justice had 30 days to provide the state with an accounting of its charitable assets and was barred from distributing or spending them without the attorney general's prior written approval. The years of noncompliance culminated in another notice from California regulators on June 19, 2026, reiterating the outstanding asset-accounting requirement and warning that Arc of Justice couldn’t distribute or spend charitable assets without the attorney general's written approval. The notice said Arc of Justice would also have to provide regulators with enough information to assure the state that there had been "no loss of charitable assets" if it sought to have its registration reinstated. The Network Contagion Research Institute previously detailed Arc of Justice's regulatory problems in a May report examining the foundation's finances and activities. FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS David Levitt, an attorney representing Arc of Justice, said the foundation has submitted filings seeking reinstatement with California regulators. The Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital on Sept. 3, 2026, that it had not received the required accounting of Arc's charitable assets. At the time, Arc was listed as "REVOKED" and "PAST DUE." As of Sept. 9, its registration remained "REVOKED," while its reporting status had changed to "IN REVIEW." California's reinstatement rules require a revoked charity to explain why it failed to comply with reporting requirements and respond to Registry notices. Laurie Styron, CEO and executive director of nonprofit watchdog CharityWatch, said Arc's substantial assets made the compliance failures difficult to explain. "A foundation with tens of millions of dollars in charitable assets certainly has the resources to comply with basic reporting requirements," she said. Fox News Digital asked Levitt to provide documentation of the reinstatement filings and to explain specifically why Arc of Justice failed to make the required California filings in the first place. He had not responded to those questions by publication time. New nonprofit surfaces in Florida California's latest compliance notice to Arc of Justice came just six weeks after a new Arc of Justice surfaced in Florida. On May 8, Barry and other people associated with the original foundation incorporated a new nonprofit bearing the same name in the Little River neighborhood in North Miami. The timing raised obvious questions: Was the California foundation moving to Florida after its charitable registration was revoked, and what was happening to its assets? The Attorney General's Office told Fox News Digital it had not received notice from Arc of Justice of any planned transfer, merger or dissolution and had not approved any transfer of the foundation's assets. Levitt told Fox News Digital that the Florida corporation was created as a "placeholder" while Arc considered relocating its operations from California, but the move was never completed. He said the California corporation was never formally wound down, no assets were transferred and the Florida entity "holds no assets and has conducted no business." "Arc of Justice, the California nonprofit corporation, currently still holds the assets," Levitt said, adding that they remain professionally managed "in the same accounts they have been in for years." Levitt subsequently provided Fox News Digital with financial documentation that independently verified that the California foundation continues to hold the assets. The Miami address wasn't new. The original Arc of Justice had been using Barry's property on its federal tax filings since at least 2017, even as it remained incorporated in California. Federal filing questions Questions have also emerged about the original foundation's federal filings. Arc of Justice's Forms 990-PF for 2023 and 2024 were not publicly available in the IRS database when Fox News Digital searched for them. Levitt subsequently provided Fox News Digital with copies of both returns. According to Levitt, Arc of Justice's accountant said both returns had been paper-filed and electronically filed, although Fox News Digital has not independently verified when the IRS received or accepted them. Benjamin was adamant in a phone interview with Fox News Digital that Arc of Justice had filed its returns every year. "I'm 100% positive. We have filed the 990s every single year," Benjamin said. She also told Fox News Digital she would make sure the missing returns were provided, which they subsequently were. Benjamin was less certain about the foundation's California regulatory problems, saying she had moved to Florida and that "the lawyer knows more than I do." After reviewing the newly produced returns, Sternal said the documents showed Arc of Justice's accountant had at least made an effort to file them, but said questions remained over whether and when they were actually submitted. "Maybe they are trying to get back into compliance with the IRS," Sternal said. "They still have a lot of clean up to do with California." Styron similarly said determining when the returns were actually filed was critical to assessing Arc of Justice's compliance. She noted that IRS and state databases can lag behind submissions but said delays of several years would be unusual. "It would be tough to say more without knowing when forms were signed and filed," Styron said. While the new records accounted for the foundation's assets and provided the previously unavailable returns, questions remained over when the federal returns were actually filed. Styron also said Arc of Justice's explanation for creating the Florida nonprofit did not absolve the California foundation's board of its responsibility to file the active organization's required forms on time. Meanwhile, Sternal, who is now a nonprofit tax attorney at law firm Holtzman Vogel who advises nonprofit and tax-exempt organizations, said there is nothing wrong or unusual about forming a nonprofit in another state. What raises questions, he said, is whether the new Florida organization is intended to take over the original foundation or its assets — a move that would trigger additional legal requirements. "It's not so easy," Sternal said. "It can be done, it's possible, but there are a lot of hoops that they have to jump through." Because Arc of Justice remained a California corporation, Sternal said it would have to work with California's attorney general before transferring funds to another organization or moving the foundation out of state. Same name, new home Along with the new Florida corporation bearing the same Arc of Justice name and Miami address used by the embattled California foundation, two of its three officers also held positions with the original organization. Maya Danaher, Benjamin's daughter and former treasurer of the original Arc of Justice, is president of the new Florida corporation. Jonathan Raggett, who served as secretary of the original foundation, is now its treasurer. Benjamin served as president of the original California foundation but is not listed as an officer of the new Florida corporation. Meanwhile, Benjamin's longtime partner, Barry, was not listed as an officer of the original foundation but serves as secretary of the new organization. He is also listed as incorporating Arc of Justice in Florida and serves as its registered agent. Its stated goal is blunt: "WE ARE HERE TO SUPPORT SOCIAL JUSTICE NON PROFITS," according to the articles of incorporation. All three officers list the Miami house as their address — a 1,334-square-foot Miami duplex owned by Barry, property records show. When Fox News Digital visited last month, the small, turquoise-blue, single-story house sat partially obscured by thick palms and tropical plants behind a weathered, multicolored wooden fence. Fading artwork of colorful cats, pigs, flowers, hearts and peace symbols covered the fence, including a pink pig holding a "ONE LOVE" sign. A large "PEACE" poster hung on the house, while a turquoise-shaded canopy stretched across the property. Two campaign signs for Democrat Kendrick Meek Jr., who unsuccessfully ran in the Democratic primary election for Florida's 24th Congressional District, stood outside. Google Street View images from 2022 show the property in brighter colors before the paint faded and vegetation obscured parts of the fence. The images also show a small white van with its front bumper missing parked outside, with "CODEPINK" written across its side in pink marker along with the Spanish words "Cuba vive y trabaja" — "Cuba lives and works." The van was not visible when Fox News Digital visited. The house's number was painted vertically on the weathered front gate — the same address listed by the original California foundation and the newly incorporated Florida Arc of Justice. SUBPOENAED PRO-CHINA OUTLET DEFENDS ITSELF ON DEMOCRACY NOW!, WHICH PAID SINGHAM-FOUNDED COMPANY MILLIONS Where did the money come from? Arc of Justice was formerly known as The Benjamin Fund, Inc., with California corporate records showing the foundation formally changed its name in November 2019. Its fortune was built largely on Benjamin family money. Benjamin's father, Alvin Benjamin, was a prominent Long Island real estate developer who founded The Benjamin Companies in the early 1960s. The Benjamin Fund's initial 2003 IRS return shows he contributed a partnership interest valued at $683,715 to the foundation, with Medea Susan Benjamin serving as president. Much larger contributions followed. In 2010, the estate of Benjamin's mother, Rose Benjamin, contributed $10,863,060, according to the foundation's IRS filing. Five years later, the Estate of Alvin Benjamin contributed another $15 million, followed by another $8,603,450 in 2019. The foundation's wealth also grew through its investments. In 2020, Arc of Justice reported $12,344,501 in unrealized gains on securities, helping push its year-end assets to nearly $40 million. Medea Benjamin — identified as Susan Benjamin on the filing — personally contributed $1 million to Arc of Justice in 2022, listing the Miami house as her address. The foundation subsequently became a vehicle for funding activist organizations, including Global Exchange, the advocacy group Benjamin co-founded with her then-husband, Kevin Danaher. The organization remains active today, with Danaher still serving on its board, according to its 2024 Form 990. Benjamin later co-founded CodePink in 2002 with Evans and has remained one of the anti-war group's most prominent activists and public faces. Arc of Justice would go on to pour substantial sums into CodePink, including $251,500 in 2020 and $355,350 in 2022, according to the foundation's IRS filings. The newly obtained returns show that Arc of Justice gave CodePink $277,580 in 2023 and another $350,000 in 2024. CodePink has itself come under federal scrutiny. Benjamin traveled to Cuba in March with fellow CodePink co-founder Evans and far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker as part of a roughly 170-person convoy to the communist-run island. Benjamin later confirmed that the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control, which enforces U.S. sanctions against Cuba, sent CodePink a detailed inquiry seeking information about the trip's financing, logistics, participants and activities. Benjamin said the group brought about $600,000 worth of humanitarian aid to Cuba and described the Treasury inquiry as "serious," while also calling it an "intimidation tactic." Evans and a network of nonprofits funded by her husband, Singham, have also come under congressional and federal scrutiny. Singham, an American tech entrepreneur who sold his software company ThoughtWorks for an estimated $785 million in 2017 and now lives in Shanghai, has directed at least $278 million into six core nonprofits that Fox News Digital previously reported promote socialist, communist and pro-China causes as part of a broader international network of media organizations, activist groups and think tanks. CodePink is one of those nonprofits. The congressional investigation remains ongoing, while Singham is separately under federal criminal investigation. Neither Singham nor CodePink has been charged with wrongdoing in connection with the investigations described here. Same name, separate entity Florida officials confirmed the new Arc of Justice was created as a Florida nonprofit on May 8, 2026, rather than simply registering the existing California corporation in the state. "That entity is on our records as a Domestic Nonprofit corporation. It is a Florida entity," Florida Department of State regulatory specialist LaCori Brown told Fox News Digital. The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services separately told Fox News Digital that the new Arc of Justice isn’t currently registered to solicit charitable contributions in the state and has not applied for a charitable solicitation registration or exemption. The department also said it hasn’t received any filings identifying assets transferred from the California Arc of Justice to the new Florida corporation nor any complaints, referrals or regulatory inquiries concerning the new organization. Sternal stressed that the available records don’t establish that Arc of Justice's assets were misappropriated or improperly used. He said the foundation's years of California noncompliance remained highly unusual. "This organization with this large endowment has simply fallen off the radar, as it were, with its filings, with its compliance with California," Sternal said. "Those don't belong to the officers and directors of the foundation. Those belong to the foundation," Sternal said. "They must be used for public charitable purposes." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Levitt said Arc of Justice's board is still considering moving the foundation out of California and potentially establishing two separate charitable vehicles so the foundation's founder and its officers and directors can pursue separate charitable activities. For now, the original Arc of Justice remains a California corporation and continues to hold its assets, while the future of the newly incorporated Florida organization remains unsettled.

articles.body:
The Michigan Senate race looks to be a near dead heat between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, according to a new poll.

The survey, which Detroit’s WDIV-TV and The Detroit News conducted from Aug. 31 to Sept. 3, found Rogers holding a slight lead over El-Sayed, with 45.8 percent support to the Democrat’s 44.4 percent.

The edge for Rogers, who represented the Wolverine State’s 8th Congressional District for 14 years, was within the margin of error of 4 percentage points.

More than 9 percent of respondents were still undecided, with early voting in Michigan starting Oct. 24.

El-Sayed and Rogers are battling to succeed outgoing two-term Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.). The race represents the GOP’s most likely pickup opportunity , as it is the only Democratic-held seat the Cook Political Report rates as a toss-up; President Trump won the state in two of his three presidential runs.

The election handicapper puts five Republican-held seats in that column , as Democrats are trying to flip a net of four seats to retake control of the upper chamber. With a 53-47 split in the Senate, Republicans can afford to see their numbers reduced by three and still maintain their majority with Vice President Vance as the tiebreaker.

As of Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ gave El-Sayed a 66 percent chance to win. That is a shift from Aug. 13, when the Democrat had a 51 percent chance to beat Rogers.

El-Sayed, a progressive former Wayne County health official, has campaigned on Medicare for All and investing more in local communities instead of on foreign wars.

“One of the things you’ll hear me talk about all the time is, I don’t want to fight stupid wars. I want to invest … in infrastructure, water infrastructure being one of those things,” El-Sayed told Michiganders last week, as captured on C-SPAN cameras.

Rogers, meanwhile, has gone after El-Sayed for campaigning with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. The former congressman has also labeled his opponent, who is Muslim, as “anti-American.”

Rogers said last week , “This guy is too extreme for … the great state of Michigan.”

articles.summary: Fox Business host Larry Kudlow on Tuesday told Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) that he “might want to think” about launching a bid for the presidency in November. Kudlow asked the Texas senator about whether or not he will run for the Republican nomination for president in 2028 in an appearance on the host’s show. “So,…
articles.body:
Fox Business host Larry Kudlow on Tuesday told Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) that he “might want to think” about launching a bid for the presidency in November.

Kudlow asked the Texas senator about whether or not he will run for the Republican nomination for president in 2028 in an appearance on the host’s show.

“So, what I will say is there will be plenty of time to have that conversation after the midterms,” Cruz answered. “We’re less than 60 days out from the midterms, so my focus –– if we lose the House and Senate, all the legislative progress we have grinds to a halt, and it is two years of warfare against President Trump and his agenda.”

Kudlow noted how Trump declared his candidacy right after the 2022 midterms and credited that to his success in 2024.

“I’m just putting it out there,” he said. “You might want to think about it. I mean, right after he did that, a lot of people scratched their heads, and it turns out that was a close outbid. It really was.”

Cruz previously ran for president in 2016 and at one point was seen as a front-runner. He won 11 state contests, including the Iowa caucuses, before suspending his campaign as Trump built a large delegate lead.

The Texan eventually backed President Trump in the general election, though he did not endorse him at the GOP’s convention in Cleveland that summer, and was then booed by Trump supporters .

At the time, Cruz reportedly told allies that he thought there was something “fundamentally wrong” with evangelical voters backing Trump. Then-candidate Trump threatened to “ spill the beans ” on Cruz’s wife, Heidi Cruz, and reposted an unflattering photo of her compared with one of first lady Melania Trump, and he claimed there was “ voter fraud ” in his loss to Cruz in Iowa.

The Texas senator is seen as a Republican contender for president in 2028 and has said the GOP has not coalesced around Vice President Vance as the party’s presidential nominee.

“There’s going to be a full discussion about who we are and what we believe,” Cruz told MS NOW’s Ali Vitali late last month when asked if the party has settled on Vance.

Cruz added that the GOP was in “the midst of a debate about who our party is,” noting that there will be “time to figure” out his role in that future.

Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who ran against Cruz and Trump in 2016, are seen as favorites to possibly succeed Trump. Neither has said publicly whether they will run in 2028, but both of their names are mentioned as potential GOP contenders.

A recent Emerson College poll showed Rubio outperforming Vance in multiple hypothetical 2028 presidential match-ups against Democratic candidates.

articles.title: How to wreck America in 20 months
articles.summary: In 20 months, Donald Trump has probably done more damage to this nation than many of our enemies.
articles.body:
With the 25th anniversary of the attack on New York’s Twin Towers days away, Osama bin Laden, along with Adolf Hitler, Vladimir Lenin and Joseph Stalin, must be rolling in their graves. All their attempts to defeat America failed. Yet, in 20 months, Donald Trump has probably done more damage to this nation than many of our enemies. Despite his reference to being the “greatest American president ever,” reminiscent of Muhammad Ali’s boast , the opposite is the case.

His supporters will cite, uncritically and robotically, all the things Trump has done as great successes. Yes, Trump did, for the most part, close the border . In his first administration, he did put in place the Abraham Accords that at least moved slightly closer to resolving some of the endemic issues that have unraveled the region for decades, if not centuries. But consider just some of the damage he has imposed.

Incredibly, Trump removed the checks and balances of the Constitution. The congressional powers outlined in Article I and Article III have been bypassed. Article II’s executive powers have been replaced by the transformation of the presidency into the sole arm of government. A Republican Congress has so far proven to have less standing than a mere rubber stamp , although that may be changing, as even some of the most MAGA of members are sensing all is not well.

Although the Supreme Court has occasionally checked the president, that has been the exception. Government is now by executive orders, of which Trump has issued 279 . When the court found tariffs to be unconstitutional , Trump discovered a loophole that had not been closed. And despite Trump’s unbridled support of tariffs, they are harming not only the U.S. — costing U.S. families, on average, around $1,300 more per year in 2026 — but also global economies. And now Trump is engaging in a trade war with the biggest U.S. trading partner, Canada.

While birthright citizenship is unambiguously stated in the Constitution , Trump is using executive orders as a work around. Seemingly a small issue, unilaterally and probably illegally, Trump demolished the East Wing to build a ballroom. Although he p romised the project would be funded by private donors , the government will now be assuming construction costs.

Domestically, both parties have become far more isolated and destructive in treating the opposition not as equals but as enemies to be destroyed. Arguably, not since the Civil War and Vietnam has the U.S. public been so divided. And the depths of the divisions may be even greater.

Trump has turned the presidency into a money printing machine . His wealth has increased by a few billion, largely through crypto. After accusing the Bidens of being a “ crime family ,” how much money has been siphoned to his sons and son-in-law, with billions of Saudi and Gulf states money to manage? And how much is Donald Trump Jr. making from Pentagon contracts and work that would not be available to someone lacking the last name of Trump?

Regarding foreign and defense policy, Trump has rejected and ruined 80 years of bipartisanship and general adherence to common themes. The record is not unblemished. However since rebuilding Germany, Japan and Europe after World War II, the U.S. has been a beacon of freedom and opportunity.

America has embraced and depended upon allies, friends and partners. From 1949 until now, NATO was the greatest military alliance in history. Trump has gone out of his way to bully and threaten NATO members to spend more on defense, or else. U.S. forces are being withdrawn or redeployed from NATO countries. Demands to take over Greenland were deeply absurd, offensive and impossible to achieve.

The result is that the alliance has been severely weakened by these policies and by Trump’s seeming embrace of Russian president Vladimir Putin. His disrespectful treatment of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the withholding of support from the Russia-Ukraine war — forcing Europe to do more — has aided Russia. And one can observe that Trump’s rekindling of his bromance with North Korea’s dictator Kim Jong Un has not gone down well with our treaty partners in the South.

Worse, after Nicolas Maduro’s capture , the U.S. has blundered into a quagmire in the Gulf. About two-thirds of Americans oppose the war in Iran, which was reportedly launched based on misleading intelligence from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Unless strong remedial diplomatic action starts now, this war could make the wars in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan seem like successes.

Harlan Ullman is senior adviser at Washington’s Atlantic Council, chairman of a private company, and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former UK chief of defense and due out this Fall, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos. “
