articles.body:
Top Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro said the White House complained to Fox News leadership about the network’s decision to oust host Maria Bartiromo last week.

“But suffice it to say that Suzanne Scott got a call, and basically the White House let her know that that kind of thing is totally unacceptable,” Navarro said, referring to Fox News CEO, during a Tuesday appearance on Newsmax.

After Bartiromo and the network parted ways abruptly last week, several news outlets reported the host shared details of internal editorial directives with officials in the White House.

“She just went out and fired Maria Bartiromo,” Navarro said of Scott. “And that place is out of control.”

Fox gave few details about Bartiromo’s ouster last week, only thanking her for “her work over the last 12 1/2 years” and wishing her “all the best on her next chapter.”

Navarro suggested there is an anti-Trump sentiment among Fox producers and reporters.

“When you craft your segments for like the equivalent of Greg Kelly every day, whatever the show is, it’s like, you don’t do these MAGA issues, you don’t do pro-Trump stuff,” he said.

Fox features a number of primetime and daytime hosts who are vocally supportive of the president and regularly carries his speeches and rallies extensively.

One of the network’s top financial news personalities, Bartiromo was among the president’s most vocal supporters on Fox’s roster of hosts and routinely backed his policies relating to the economy and trade.

President Trump mourned her departure from Fox in a Truth Social post last week, writing he “can’t believe” she is no longer at the network and adding “her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy.”

articles.title: LEE CARTER: The summer polls missed the point: Voters are moving — and the midterms begin
articles.summary: Summer polls carry a giant asterisk as the real midterm electorate forms now, with grocery prices and checkout costs driving the key voter concerns.
articles.body: If you think you know who’s winning the midterms, I have some bad news. The voters who will decide them are just starting to pay attention. I say this as someone who loves polls. They tell us what people care about, what they’re worried about and where the political opportunities are. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: VOTERS SAY THEY’RE IN ECONOMIC PAIN, BUT WILL DEMOCRATS GAIN? But summer horse-race numbers come with a giant asterisk: The electorate isn’t finished yet. We saw it all summer. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed appeared headed toward a comfortable Democratic Senate primary victory. He won by about a point. LEE CARTER: ELECTION SHOCKER: THE WINNERS HAD A SLOGAN; THE LOSERS JUST HAD RÉSUMÉS In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong led David Crowley by roughly 20 points in two polls. Crowley won. In Minnesota, a public poll had Angie Craig ahead of Peggy Flanagan by two. Flanagan won by nearly 20. 100 DAYS UNTIL MIDTERMS AND DEMOCRATS ARE WINNING BECAUSE THEY ACTUALLY HAVE A MESSAGE The lesson isn’t that polls are wrong. It’s that voters move. And now comes the part of the campaign when they start moving. Labor Day is the unofficial beginning of the election season for the people who don’t spend August obsessing over politics. Which is to say: most people. They don’t know who won the week. They didn’t see the viral clip. They aren’t refreshing the generic ballot. They have never described themselves as "low-propensity voters." They’re busy. And politics has developed a very bad habit of confusing the people who are paying the most attention with the people who will ultimately decide the election. CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION We confuse loud with large. A few thousand furious people can generate an enormous amount of internet. Millions of people wondering why their grocery bill is still so high can generate almost none. Then Election Day comes along and counts them exactly the same. This is why I’m less interested in who moved from 47 to 48 this week than in what sits underneath the number. REDISTRICTING GIVES REPUBLICANS AN EDGE, BUT AFFORDABILITY WILL DECIDE THE MIDTERMS Who is certain? Who is movable? Who is going to vote? And which party is actually reaching people who weren’t already with them? Because there is a huge difference between making your supporters more enthusiastic and turning more people into your supporters. Attention feels like momentum. Persuasion creates it. Which makes what Republicans are doing in Dallas this week fascinating. For the first time, the GOP is holding a national convention built around a midterm election. They wanted the stage. They got it. Now the question is whether they use it to talk to themselves or to the voters they still need. DAVID MARCUS: EXPERTS CROWNED EL-SAYED — THEN MICHIGAN VOTERS TURNED HIS WIN INTO A NEAR-DISASTER Because Republicans don’t have an awareness problem. Everyone knows Donald Trump. They don’t have an enthusiasm problem among their most loyal supporters. They have an affordability problem. 100 DAY SPRINT TO THE MIDTERMS KICKS OFF AS REPUBLICANS AND DEMOCRATS CLASH FOR CONTROL ACROSS THE COUNTRY Americans don’t experience the economy through a press release. They experience it at checkout. Washington has statistics. Americans have receipts. They know what groceries cost. They know what happened to their insurance premium. They know what the electric bill looks like. They know whether a decent salary suddenly doesn’t feel so decent anymore. Republicans can spend their time in Dallas explaining why the economy is better. Or they can answer the question voters are actually asking: When does my life get more affordable? That’s the opening. RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS SUMMER TRAVEL SEASON ENDS, MIDTERMS LOOM AND IRAN WAR WAGES ON And Democrats see it too. Texas Democrat James Talarico is counterprogramming the Republican convention with a statewide food drive focused on grocery prices and affordability. It’s almost painfully perfect. Republicans have the arena. Democrats want the grocery cart. That’s the midterm fight. Republicans can use Dallas to make people who already love Trump cheer louder. Or they can give people who aren’t sold on Republicans a reason to reconsider. One produces a great television moment. The other produces votes. And that’s what I’ll be watching in every poll from here to November. Not simply who is ahead. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Who is moving? Who is persuadable? Who is expanding their coalition? Who is turning concern into choice and enthusiasm into turnout? The political class spent the summer measuring attention. Now we get to measure something much more important. Persuasion. The midterms start now. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Republicans go first. Get the popcorn. articles.title: Elections won’t fix America’s political divisions
articles.summary: If you think politics in America could not be more acrimonious than it is right now, don’t bet on it. It’s about to get much worse, unless we, the American people, do something about it.
articles.body:
If you think politics in America could not be more acrimonious than it is right now, don’t bet on it. It’s about to get much worse, unless we, the American people, do something about it.

It is difficult to know whether the seemingly irresolvable partisan divide in Congress causes or merely reflects the divides in our society. Either way, there used to be a moderate middle occupied by liberal Republicans and conservative Democrats. This middle disappeared long before President Trump entered politics. By 2020, his fourth year in office, the nation’s 10 most polarized years had occurred over the previous 16 years, across both Democratic and Republican administrations.

The historical perspective can be helpful. America’s cohesion is not based on common ethnicity, religion or ancient history. It is based on the ideals of liberty, equality, God-given rights, and government with the consent of the people.

The social contract holds those ideals together day by day. It respects that common ground does not require common opinions. We don’t have to agree on everything. In fact, we never will — not in a democracy like ours that guarantees freedom of religion, thought and expression. Instead, the contract requires a shared allegiance to civic duty, civility and mutual respect. It not only allows but also celebrates the coexistence of diverse, even competing, ideologies.

The failure to honor that contract has previously split social cohesion. The Civil War was the most violent example. Americans united to help fight World War II, and enjoyed growing prosperity as we created the middle class in the post-war years. But it wasn’t long before events tested the contract again.

The Civil Rights Movement , whose roots were deep, won legal victories in the mid-1950s. Millions of Americans surged into the streets in the 1960s to demonstrate for civil and women’s rights, environmental protections and an end to the “endless” Vietnam War. It was a profoundly disillusioning period when the American people learned they could no longer trust the president of the United States. There was Watergate, but also the president’s decision, for political reasons , to prolong the Vietnam War long after he knew we could not win it. Tens of thousands of U.S. soldiers were killed as a result.

So, although Trump did not plant the seeds of today’s divisions, he has accelerated them with gross, escalating violations of the American compact, the Constitution, the law, and the norms that have sustained trust between a president and the people. He is working actively to undermine confidence in elections , the most fundamental tool by which citizens consent to and control government. We cannot predict exactly what Trump might do to maintain power during the final legal years of his presidency, but what we know of him tells us he would rather burn down the White House than be forced out of it.

This year’s midterm elections will not end Trump’s threats, heal the nation’s political polarity, or restore civility. Elections typically reflect the nation’s differences rather than heal them. Civil society is fragmented. Americans once joined unions, churches, service clubs, fraternal organizations and neighborhood groups. By 2024, an American Social Capital Survey found that fewer than one in five Americans participate in neighborhood, sports, workout and similar groups.

Change.org is a website that invites people to create and circulate petitions. As one such petition states: “We disagree on politics, religion, immigration, education, economics, and countless other issues. Yet beneath those differences, most of us want many of the same things. … Imagine neighborhoods filled with people who choose service over outrage, curiosity over assumptions, collaboration over division, and courage over complacency.”

It will take work. The Pew Research Center found last year that only 34 percent of Americans believe most people can be trusted, and only 44 percent trust all or most of their neighbors. On the other hand, three in four would water an absent neighbor’s plants or take food to a sick person. We see that spirit emerge during personal and collective disasters. Two-thirds of Americans believe they can learn something valuable by connecting with people who are different from themselves, and 70 percent feel they have a responsibility to make those connections. Asked why they don’t do it more, most cited a lack of opportunity.

Clergyman and peace activist William Sloane Coffin once wrote , “All human beings have more in common than they have in conflict, and it is precisely when what they have in conflict seems overriding that what they have in common needs most to be affirmed.”

November will change the composition of Congress. The 2028 election will produce a new president. But only the people can make the country great.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “ Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “ Democracy in a Hotter Time .” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Congress must get healthcare price transparency right
articles.summary: Author Jordan Smith Hart argues that Congress should pass the stronger Senate version of healthcare price transparency legislation to prevent patients from facing manufactured financial crises.
articles.body:
When I was 21 years old, I drove to the nearest hospital with a leg swollen to the size of a toddler. After hours of pokes, prods and scans, I learned I had a blood clot that was dangerously close to killing me.

Shockingly, that was not the most frightening news of the night.

As a terrified college student, I asked anyone who would listen: how much is this going to cost me? After repeated shakes of the head and assertions that “it didn’t matter,” one hospital worker gave me the brutal answer: $18,000, at least. Forget the blood clot — that number gave me a panic attack.

I had no way of knowing at the time, but that devastating price tag wasn’t real. I later asked the hospital to itemize the exact price of my treatments; it turns out my bill would come out to less than $900 if I paid in cash. But in the convoluted world of healthcare pricing, the hospital was planning to charge my insurance company so much more. The insurer later negotiated it down, but the bill still came out to thousands of dollars, not the much lower cash price.

I’ve been thinking about this traumatic experience as the House and Senate debate legislation on price transparency. Both chambers — and strong majorities of both parties — want to give patients an honest look at real costs with the goal of making healthcare more affordable and shoppable. So does President Trump, who has issued an executive order on price transparency and wants legislation to lock in even stronger reforms.

The case for legislative change couldn’t be more clear. While my experience wouldn’t be covered by price transparency, due to existing laws on surprise billing, it nonetheless shows the healthcare system hides and drives up costs for everyday patients. Hospitals and providers manufacture sky-high prices for the treatments they provide only for insurance companies to negotiate prices down. But nearly half the time , the cash price is lower than the median price insurers negotiate.

This payment system is backward. No American would agree to buy a car, a television or even a t-shirt without knowing the price first. That knowledge sparks the competition that drives down prices. Health care does the opposite, hiding prices on the front-end while encouraging providers and insurers to drive up costs behind the scenes. Health care billing should operate like every other product or service, with transparent cash prices disclosed upfront, so Americans can protect their health and their wallets.

Lawmakers in both the House and the Senate understand this, but unfortunately, the bills they’re debating aren’t created equal.

The Senate bill — the Patients Deserve Price Tags Act — is stronger. It requires that accurate procedure and treatment pricing be disclosed in real dollars upfront. It covers more medical providers and it prevents federal agencies from issuing waivers. In short, the Senate wants to make price transparency real and enforceable.

But the House bill — the Lower Costs, More Transparency Act — falls short. It leaves loopholes and carveouts that continue the status quo. When a price isn’t a fixed dollar amount, it lets that price stay buried in a formula instead of requiring the formula to be disclosed. It covers fewer providers, offers more exemptions, and allows for waivers that a future administration would surely use to gut the reform altogether. Joe Biden failed to fully enforce President Trump’s 2019 regulation on price transparency. Waivers would allow a future president to effectively disregard an entire federal law.

For the sake of Americans, the House and Senate must agree to codify the strongest possible bill. While the Senate language gives this reform the best shot at airtight implementation, it could also be improved. The House is also debating the CHECK Act , which would expose how health-plan middlemen and their affiliates get paid, guarantee patients a clear explanation of benefits, and require the bills they receive to be plainly itemized. That reform is worth including in the final bill, so Americans know exactly what they are paying for and why.

No one should face a financial scare in healthcare, least of all over a manufactured crisis. For me, the panic I felt when I heard the price of my care was $18,000 somehow felt worse than the blood clot itself.

Only the strongest law will protect future patients going into doctors’ offices, getting scans, or receiving treatments to save their lives. For the sake of their wellbeing as well as their wallet, Americans deserve nothing less than full and total price transparency.

Jordan Smith Hart is federal affairs director at the Foundation for Government Accountability.

articles.title: ‘Trump-a-palooza’ kicks off in Texas
articles.summary: Plus: 🤔Is Jimmy Kimmel staying with ABC? {beacon} It’s Wednesday, and the wait is over for football fans. The NFL regular season kicks off tonight! In today’s issue: Day 1 of RNC convention Rhode Island elections Oil, gas prices soar Super Bowl rematch Programming note: We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker, filling in…
articles.body:
It’s Wednesday, and the wait is over for football fans. The NFL regular season kicks off tonight!

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com.

The GOP will host its first midterms convention in Dallas, Texas on Wednesday afternoon. President Trump will headline the two-day event, which Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters has labelled “Trump-a-palooza.”

Prepare for a busy couple nights. The event has 100 speeches, presentations and performances listed on its schedule.

Wednesday’s speakers will include Attorney General Todd Blanche , Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Texas Attorney General and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton (R).

Programming will also feature candidates from key swing districts and federal immigration enforcement officers.

Meanwhile, Democrats will hold their own rally in Dallas , House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced Friday.

“Americans are being crushed by rising costs. Republicans don’t care—they’re in Dallas, celebrating an out of touch President whose tariffs and wars are making things worse. We’re going to hold them accountable,” wrote Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.), who will attend the Democratic counterprogramming, on the social platform X.

📅 The full slate: Look at the full schedule of Wednesday’s RNC convention speakers below (All times EDT):

4-5 p.m.: RNC Chair Joe Gruters , Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas) and House candidate Carlos De La Cruz (R-Texas), Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) Housing and Urban Development Sec. Scott Turner and Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.)

5-6 p.m. : House Majority Leader Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), House Majority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.), Republican Attorneys General Association Chair AG Austin Knudsen (R-Mont.), North Carolina Senate nominee Michael Whatley (R) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.)

6-7 p.m. : Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), Texas Attorney General and Senate nominee Ken Paxton (R) and Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.)

7-8 p.m. : Sen. John Husted (R-Ohio), Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), Adam Carolla , Georgia GOP Senate nominee Rep. Mike Collins, Oklahoma lieutenant governor nominee T.W. Shannon (R) and Attorney General Todd Blanche .

8-9 p.m. : Centers for Medicaid and Medicare Services Admin Dr. Mehmet Oz , Florida GOP Gov. Nominee Byron Donalds , GOP House nominees Jay Feely (Ariz.) and Mike Bouchard (Mich.), Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , UFC fighters Bo Nickal and Justin Gaethje

RAISED EYEBROWS : The president on Tuesday criticized New York Magazine for its coverage of the president’s retelling of his experience during terrorist attacks.

Trump in a speech said he was near the U.S. Steel Building in New York City when two firefighters picked him up from the ground.

“Everything I said was exactly accurate and, to prove the point, I am attaching clips of me there with numerous of my people,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

CNN’s Daniel Dale with a good rundown of what we know about Trump’s 9/11 whereabouts.

The Ocean State will hold its Democratic gubernatorial primary today (yeah, Wednesday primary, weird), featuring a rematch between incumbent Gov. Dan McKee and former CVS executive Helena Foulkes .

The two Democrats previously faced off in 2022, with McKee edging Foulkes by 3 percentage points, but this year’s race appears to face a decent gap in the other direction, according to The Hill’s Caroline Vakil .

Troubled waters : A major highlight of the race is the slow reconstruction of Rhode Island’s westbound Washington Bridge.

Residents have grown frustrated over how long it has taken to rebuild the bridge after it was closed three years ago due to structural issues. Just about all fingers have been pointed at McKee for the slow process.

“I know there is a lot of frustration, and I accept it,” McKee told The New York Times. “But in the end, people are going to realize we did the right thing.”

Whoever wins Tuesday’s primary will be the heavy favorite in November against either Aaron Guckian or Elaine Pelino .

GOP gears up for fight in New Hampshire:

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) and former Sen. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) on Tuesday won their respective primary races to fill outgoing Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-N.H.) seat.

New Hampshire has not elected a Republican senator in more than 15 years, but recent polls have the GOP feeling hopeful about a potential flip.

“From now until November, SLF will spend every day highlighting John E. Sununu’s positive vision for New Hampshire while exposing the corruption, self-dealing, and radical record of Washington insider Chris Pappas,” said Republican-affiliated Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) Executive Director Alex Latcham in a Tuesday statement.

In April, SLF announced a $17 million reservation to boost Sununu after the primary, while Elon Musk’s America PAC has also spent in the race.

A University of New Hampshire (UNH) poll released Aug. 26, Sununu led Pappas 45 percent to 43 percent.

Senate dreams : Pappas departed his role representing New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, creating another competitive race in the Granite State.

Stefany Shaheen , daughter of Jeanne Shaheen, late last night defeated Democratic Party Vice Chair Maura Sullivan in the Democratic primary to replace Papas.

A day after the U.S. struck five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, Iran announced Wednesday that it targeted two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that the U.S. vessels attempted to pass through a restricted area. Tehran also reportedly launched strikes on a U.S. base in Jordan.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said U.S. forces will continue attacking tankers if Iran carries out additional strikes on American naval vessels.

⛽ What’s does this mean for oil and gas prices?: For the first time since July, oil prices reached over $100 a barrel in response to the continued strikes in the Middle East, with brent crude jumping about 3 percent, according to The Hill’s Finya Swai.

The price of regular gas also jumped overnight, rising 7 cents and increasing to a national average of $4.22, according to AAA.

On Sunday, when gas prices hit a record high heading into Labor Day, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that prices were more likely to go down than up.

“But if you look at the futures market right now, what can you buy gasoline for two months in advance from where we are today? It’s down more than 30 cents a gallon from where it is today,” he said on CNN’s “State of the Union” with Dana Bush.

President Trump also brushed off the rise in oil prices Monday, saying they “will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping,” when the Iran war ends.

Page Six reported on Tuesday that ABC will not be extending Jimmy Kimmel’s contract beyond 2027, putting an end to his show “Jimmy Kimmel Live.” But ABC pushed back, releasing a statement to The Hill Tuesday saying, “This information is inaccurate — any reports about the future of the show are purely speculative.”

The NCAA said it cannot overturn the result of Saturday’s controversial Western Michigan vs. Michigan game. Officials added one second to the game clock, which allowed Michigan to score a game-winning touchdown as time expired. MAC Commissioner Jon Steinbrecher asked the NCAA to declare Western Michigan “the actual winner.”

An account on the social platform X will post live updates on 9/11 as if the attacks were happening in real time to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the events. The account is called 2001 Live and curated by Manny Marotta .

President Trump gifted several White House aides — including special and executive assistant Natalie Harp — $45,000 cash gifts, according to financial disclosures released by the Trump administration.

A zoo in South Bend, Ind. just welcomed a new red panda cub in June and wants the public to help pick a name! The deadline to pick a name is Sept. 18!

articles.title: Holder blasts Blanche over planned GOP convention speech: ‘Disgraceful’
articles.summary: Former Attorney General Eric Holder on Tuesday slammed the sitting Department of Justice (DOJ) chief over his decision to address attendees at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first midterm convention in Dallas, which kicks off Wednesday. Holder, who served in the Obama administration, called Attorney General Todd Blanche’s planned speech “unprecedented” and “disgraceful” in comments…
articles.body:
Former Attorney General Eric Holder on Tuesday slammed the sitting Department of Justice (DOJ) chief over his decision to address attendees at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) first midterm convention in Dallas, which kicks off Wednesday .

Holder, who served in the Obama administration, called Attorney General Todd Blanche’s planned speech “unprecedented” and “disgraceful” in comments to The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation.

“Attorneys general don’t talk about political things,” Holder told NewsNation’s Joe Khalil. “He shouldn’t be there.”

When reached for comment about Holder’s criticism, the DOJ directed The Hill to its Wednesday response to a complaint from Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee about the upcoming remarks.

“While Jack Smith may agree with you about violating federal law, the Hatch Act is available for everyone to read, and Todd Blanche’s appearance this evening in his personal capacity is legal (and has been approved by ethics),” the department’s official social platform X account posted Wednesday.

The Democrats on the House panel called Blanche’s planned speech at the RNC convention “dumbfounding and unprecedented” in their own post Tuesday.

“Amazing how far the DOJ has fallen. We’ll be watching,” the group wrote.

Blanche is scheduled to address the convention’s attendees Wednesday evening. Other speakers include Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton (R) and several GOP members of Congress.

President Trump is also set to address attendees on both nights of the two-day event in the Lone Star State. Trump touted the convention as “the Greatest RALLY of them all” in a Truth Social post Friday.

“I’ll be speaking on night one, and hanging around for an earlier closing, and lots of music, on night two!!! See you in Dallas,” he wrote.

The president nominated Blanche , his former personal attorney, to oversee the DOJ after he fired former Attorney General Pam Bondi from the role in April. Blanche previously served as deputy attorney general and then as acting attorney general following Bondi’s departure.

Senate Democrats repeatedly grilled the attorney general over his personal relationship with the president and the “ anti-weaponization fund ” controversy during his confirmation process.

In an online statement following the Senate’s confirmation of Blanche last month, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said the attorney general “has no intention of stopping Trump’s corruption.”

“He advanced his career enabling it,” Schumer continued. “Every senator who voted to confirm him has now branded themselves as an enabler, too.”

articles.title: Merit-based and colorblind: The Pentagon’s cover story for purging Black officers
articles.summary: A veteran and academic argues that recent military leadership decisions under the Trump administration are dismantling racial equality in the armed forces by dismissing the merits of promoted Black officers.
articles.body:
I entered U.S. military service in 1964, right as Vietnam was escalating. Despite the Civil Rights Movement, roughly 31 percent of the hundreds of thousands mostly male recruits sent to the Marines and Army in 1965 were Black — this when Black men were just 10.8 percent of the U.S. male population.

Once in Vietnam, men like me, Black men, were killed in combat during that period at a staggering 25 percent rate — nearly twice what our population share would predict . I witnessed this firsthand as an Airman, one of the few Blacks in my unit. I was deployed to Da Nang where I worked in communications supporting Marine units, filled with Black faces that were conspicuously absent in my own Air Force Specialty Code (AFSC) classification.

That is not an accident of demographics. It’s because Black men who were facing the draft did not have access to the pathways to enlist in the National Guard, as many of my white classmates did. Instead, we were sent to the front lines during one of the bloodiest wars America has ever engaged.

Thanks to courageous military leaders who spoke out, the military eventually changed and became one where Black men and women had greater equality, access to opportunities, and could meaningfully advance their careers. Still, I carry that history with me, and it makes what I am watching now deeply disturbing.

Today, Black men in the military are once again experiencing a unique, racist danger. This time around, it’s the denial of advancement and promotion despite having served the U.S. military honorably, some for more than two decades. Such treatment is racist at its core, assuming that any promotion Black men earned before this administration took office must have been a function of DEI rather than demonstrated competence.

Upward mobility in the military is supposed to be straightforward, built on time-in-grade. At the junior levels, that might be two or three years each advancement; with no demerits during each interval, you advance once the time has elapsed. Higher levels work the same way, just with longer time intervals.

For officers, there are supposed to be oversight boards that review promotion recommendations before they move up the chain of command to the final signatories with approval authority. No single individual is supposed to hold the power to make or break a promotion.

While Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has declared that race and sex will no longer factor into these promotions, or military academy admissions — a “ colorblind and merit-based ” standard, in his words — it’s clear that they actually do, though not in the direction about which his comments indicated concern.

He fired Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr. , only the second Black chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in history, after more than 41 years of service. He forced out Col. Dave Butler , removing him from the brigadier general promotion list. And perhaps the clearest case of all is that of Rear Adm. Stephen D. Barnett — a career officer denied a promotion to vice admiral that, by every account of his record, he had earned. Meanwhile, a recently-circulated promotion list of roughly three dozen officers, overwhelmingly white men, advanced without comparable scrutiny .

What’s more, Hegseth has taken it upon himself to inflict pain on Black men and women who have earned every reward their service record entitles them to. Consider his public remarks about Gen. Lloyd Austin — a 40-year veteran, West Point graduate, secretary of Defense from 2021-2025, four-star general, and the 12th commander of U.S. Central Command, where he led military operations across the Middle East and Central and South Asia.

Hegseth’s dismissal — “I don’t know what Lloyd Austin did for four years” — is more than an insult. It is a familiar erasure, the same impulse that has long denied Black achievement its due, now voiced from the highest civilian office in the Pentagon.

But in the face of these insults and dismissals, there’s silence. There has been no public outcry among the many colonels and generals who surely know better. No one inside the military services has stood up publicly, on the record, to speak on behalf of their Black fellow service members. A few officers have spoken to reporters, but only anonymously. Of course, it’s well known what the Trump administration does to those who “speak up,” but if these actions go unchallenged, they will only continue.

Sadly, these cases do more than just damage the reputation and career trajectories of esteemed Black people who chose military service. They reverse the aspirational goal of President Truman’s 1948 Executive Order 9981 that desegregated the U.S. Military. That order offered a pathway to the middle class for millions of Black Americans and their families. A pathway that opened up access to achieve the American Dream despite the persistence of Jim Crow-style segregation that remained in both public and private institutions.

My military service in Vietnam earned me GI Bill benefits that paid for my college and graduate education and helped me buy my first home. The professional-class stability those benefits made possible went on to shape the upwardly mobile trajectory of the children I raised in that home.

Military service never guaranteed upward mobility for Black Americans — but the wholesale relabeling of decades of earned advancement as “favoritism” rather than merit is not mere neglect of that pathway. It is its deliberate dismantling, and Black families will pay the cost for generations to come.

Earl Smith, Ph.D., is professor and senior research scientist at the Center for the Study and Prevention of Gender-Based Violence, University of Delaware, and author of “Race, Sport and the American Dream.” He is the co-author with Dr. Angela J. Hattery of “Way Down in the Hole: Race, Intimacy and the Reproduction of Racial Ideologies in Solitary Confinement,” published in 2023 by Rutgers University Press.

articles.title: More Americans skeptical of government information: Survey
articles.summary: A new poll has found that Americans are more skeptical of information released by the federal government, with majorities saying they have little to no trust in the government. The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and USAFacts survey released Wednesday shows that almost 6 in 10 Americans say they trust the government “only…
articles.body:
A new poll has found that Americans are more skeptical of information released by the federal government, with majorities saying they have little to no trust in the government.

The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and USAFacts survey released Wednesday shows that almost 6 in 10 Americans say they trust the government “only a little” or not at all,” with 34 percent of American adults saying they trust the federal certification of election results “a great deal” or “quite a bit,” a 6-point drop since 2024.

Mistrust among Americans on most key issues has gone up, with 53 percent saying they trust “only a little” or “not at all” of the government’s information on education, 58 percent on environmental information, 57 percent on election results, 56 percent on immigration information and 46 percent on healthcare information.

Pollsters found that mistrust of nearly every topic has risen slightly since they first started asking in their 2019 survey . The latest survey found that trust in government information has declined as it has become more partisan since President Trump’s first term.

Trust in government information shifts when the opposing party controls the White House, the AP-NORC survey uncovered.

Democrats trusted government information less during Trump’s first term, though not dramatically more than Republicans. Democrats’ doubts declined under former President Biden but spiked again after Trump returned to the White House. But Republican distrust in government information saw a steady rise under Biden.

On some issues, the poll found that more Democrats, at 61 percent, have low trust in information about the federal budget, compared to 42 percent of Republicans.

A similar percentage of Democrats are skeptical about information released about crime, while 32 percent of Republicans say they feel the same.

Americans’ faith in institutions and trust in nonpartisan facets of government have waned as hyperpartisanship has increased in recent years. Information about elections has been scrutinized amid unfounded claims against election results, including during the 2020 presidential election.

Polling released by Fox News in June found that a quarter of registered voters said they “generally trust” the government, with 74 percent saying they do not. More than half of voters said they trusted the government in 2002, but that number has remained below 40 percent since the second Obama administration.

The AP-NORC survey was conducted July 29 to Aug. 10 and included 1,036 respondents. The margin of error is 4.1 percentage points.

articles.title: VP JD Vance’s socialist welfare plan exposed: Conservatives feuding!
articles.summary: Paying people to stay home and not work is in fact paying people not to work, and we don’t want that. That is a system that is begging to be taken advantage of.
articles.body:
Vice President Vance has proposed a new welfare scheme to help out families so that one parent can stay home to raise the kids while the other one works. While it’s a noble goal, it’s dividing conservatives, since the plan is in effect another big government handout.

According to reports , the plan is to take money that has already been set aside by the government, and make available $9,000 to each family that has one parent working more than 35 hours a week, and the other parent staying home with the kids.

The idea is simple: Instead of spending government money on day care services, why not just give that money to families directly? Here was rightwing commentator Benny Johnson praising the idea.

But not all conservatives were so excited about it. Meghan McCain, for instance, assailed the plan as the kind of welfare scheme Republicans typically say they are against. Similarly, conservative radio host Erick Erickson described the plan as “welfare for married people,” and further evidence that the GOP is pivoting toward becoming the socialist lite party, i.e. the “Diet Coke of Socialism.”

Well, you can probably guess my views: I’m with Erick and Meghan, and others, who view this proposal as another misguided welfare scheme.

The fact that the money was already appropriated might make it tempting to say well, if we are spending the money, we might as well spend it this way — sort of life how we support education vouchers that give the money that would be spent on public schools to the families themselves to spend on their ideal education for their kids.

I understand that, but it’s wrong. Paying people to stay home and not work is in fact paying people not to work, and we don’t want that. It is wrong, wrong, wrong, wrong to pay people not to work. That is a system that is begging to be taken advantage of.

Here’s my counter proposal: An income tax cut. A massive income tax cut. Let people keep more of what they earn, and use that money to arrange whatever the ideal child care strategy is for them.

Maybe that means mom can quit her job entirely. Maybe she works part time, and grandparents help out. Maybe there’s a full-time sitter. The point is, it’s not really the government’s job to come up with an across-the-board policy that says “here’s what’s best, let’s throw money at it.” Instead, it let people keep more of their own money, and work it out for themselves.

That would be a truly conservative limited government pro-family approach, if Republicans would just dare to dream it into being during the few weeks they have remaining with total control of the government.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Smithsonian head to resign after Trump admin threats to cut off support
articles.summary: The Smithsonian museums don’t have to tell Americans that their country is terrible to tell the truth about the terrible things America has done. And acknowledging slavery, segregation, displacement or discrimination does not erase the country’s achievements.
articles.body:
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced he will step down by the end of the year, after seven years leading one of the most important cultural institutions in the country.

Bunch is the first Black person and the first historian to lead the Smithsonian. His departure comes as the Trump administration has dramatically escalated its fight with the institution over how American history should be told.

Just days ago, the administration threatened to cut off federal agencies’ support f or the Smithsonian, including loans of artifacts, procurement assistance and discretionary grants, accusing the institution of promoting what it calls an anti-American narrative.

The administration has also accused the National Museum of American History of promoting “extreme political activism.”

And in August, President Trump was explicit about what he believes is wrong, writing on Truth Social:

“The Museums throughout Washington, but all over the Country are, essentially, the last remaining segment of ‘WOKE.’ The Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been — Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future.”

That’s untrue. I’ve been to both the American History Museum and the African American History Museum recently and both have plenty of truth, history and, yes, uplifting stories about America.

Still, American history is not one long story of triumph. It is the Declaration of Independence and slavery. It is the moon landing and Japanese internment. It is Harriet Tubman and the Underground Railroad and the institution of slavery that made an Underground Railroad necessary in the first place.

These things are not contradictions. They all are American history.

Bunch actually explained the philosophy guiding his work i n an interview with NBC earlier this year:

“The notion of being a more perfect union — not the perfect union — is really what motivates me. And I think what I want people to understand is that there is a responsibility to continue to make those aspirations available, accessible, and meaningful to a whole range of people, and that America’s greatest strength is not running away from its history, but understanding how that history shaped us and continues to shape us.”

The Smithsonian museums don’t have to tell Americans that their country is terrible to tell the truth about the terrible things America has done. And acknowledging slavery, segregation, displacement or discrimination does not erase the country’s achievements. You can’t possibly understand American freedom without understanding who was denied freedom. You can’t possibly understand why the civil rights movement was so important without understanding Jim Crow.

Bunch has largely tried to avoid turning the Smithsonian into a partisan battlefield, but the administration has continued escalating its pressure, including an executive order directing officials to remove what it calls “ improper, divisive or anti-American ideology ” from the institution. Bunch says he has “mixed emotions” about his departure and that he wants to continue protecting the integrity of the Smithsonian and championing a history that illuminates the complexity of the nation.

What the administration needs to understand is that history doesn’t become more patriotic when you remove the painful chapters. Whoever takes on this role next has a job is to preserve the evidence — all of it. The good, the bad, the inspiring and the devastating. And give Americans the opportunity to understand how all of those pieces became the country we are today.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: NYPD chief: 9/11 heroes’ legacy lives on in every generation of officers
articles.summary: The NYPD memorial wall at One Police Plaza honors 23 officers killed on 9/11 and hundreds more lost to World Trade Center-related illnesses.
articles.body: The legacy of the NYPD officers who ran toward danger on Sept. 11, 2001, continues to shape the department a quarter-century later, Chief of Department Michael LiPetri said during a ceremony dedicating a memorial wall to members who died in the attacks and their aftermath. "None of us gets here alone," LiPetri said. "Whatever rank we reach, whatever command we lead, we are standing on the foundations other people built." "We inherit their lessons, their example, and eventually it becomes our responsibility to pass those things forward," he added. FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE The NYPD has lost more than 469 members to illnesses connected to their service after the attacks, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said. More than 1,700 members have retired from the department with World Trade Center-related disabilities, LiPetri added. "We are still losing members to illnesses caused by their service after the attacks," LiPetri said. "All these years later, we are still standing with families as they bury loved ones whose lives were forever changed by the work they did after Sept. 11." 9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY The memorial wall at One Police Plaza honors the 23 NYPD officers killed at the World Trade Center that morning, along with members who later died from illnesses linked to their rescue and recovery efforts. "Sept. 11 did not end on Sept. 11," NYPD Chief Chaplain Rev. A.R. Bernard said during the invocation. "For many, the costs continued for years, illness endured, families impacted and lives ultimately lost." FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE Mayor Zohran Mamdani recalled the story of Officer John William Perry, who was at One Police Plaza preparing to resign and begin a career as an attorney when the first plane struck the North Tower. Perry asked for his shield back and rushed to the World Trade Center. "There he was confronted with unimaginable suffering, but he did not stop with the same immense bravery and courage that was commonplace among so many that day, the kind that has long defined this department," Mamdani said. "Officer Perry ran into the fire. The last time he was seen he was helping a woman out of the South Tower before rushing back in to save as many others as he could. Officer Perry and 22 of his fellow officers, each with their own stories, were killed that morning. That includes 14 members of the emergency service unit, who were among the first to enter the towers." TRUMP POSTHUMOUSLY AWARDS MEDAL OF FREEDOM TO 9/11'S 'MAN IN RED BANDANA' Mamdani noted that the sons of officers Ronnie Klopfer and Joseph Viviano "now carry on his legacy of bravery as valued members of this very department." "Every officer present that day embodied the NYPD’s creed that the duty to protect is not a job that one clocks out of, but a calling," Mamdani said. "One answers until the very end. "In the days and months that followed Sept. 11, thousands of NYPD officers and staff from across every precinct and every borough heeded that same call. They took on that same heavy and incalculable risk." REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS Their sons play on the same lacrosse team Klopfer founded before the attacks. "Their fathers are gone, but the team that Ron built is still here," LiPetri said. "Their sons are wearing an NYPD uniform, and a connection that began years before Sept. 11 continues inside the department." Tisch said thousands of current NYPD officers were children on 9/11, while many others had not yet been born. She said preserving the memories of those who served is becoming increasingly important as the generation that responded to the attacks retires. "The example of the men and women behind them will continue to shape the department."

articles.title: Bipartisan duo launches congressional caucus to confront antisemitism at colleges
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Elise Stefanik of New York and Democratic Rep. Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey are launching the Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus.
articles.body: Reps. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y. and Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., are launching a congressional coalition to target antisemitism at institutions of higher education. The Combating Antisemitism on College Campuses Caucus will provide a bipartisan avenue for lawmakers to "coordinate oversight of how" schools of higher learning react to antisemitism, according to press releases issued by the lawmakers' offices. The caucus will "press institutions to protect Jewish students, faculty, and staff, and to enforce their own anti-harassment and anti-discrimination policies," "advance and track federal legislation targeting campus antisemitism and BDS-driven discrimination," and "spotlight schools that are getting it right and share best practices across campuses nationwide," the releases note. "Since October 7th, Jewish students on too many campuses have been harassed, intimidated, and made to feel like strangers in their own school," Gottheimer said, referring to the 2023 attack by Hamas terrorists in Israel. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Ahead of GOP convention, Dallas Dems share worried optimism
articles.summary: James Talarico faces an enthusiasm gap at the Dallas Labor Day rally as his Texas senate race against Ken Paxton heats up with new ad money.
articles.body: There were a few hundred Democrats gathered at a venue called Lofty Spaces in Dallas on Monday, in a sweltering heat that could not hold back the annual Labor Day political rally. And while on the surface all was confidence, when you scratched a little deeper, you struck frayed nerves. Ellen, a retired nurse who sometimes protests in a Statue of Liberty costume, was there, and agreed to an interview if I helped to take her gear to her car, which I would have done anyway, of course. Ellen was optimistic about Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in his race against Republican Ken Paxton. "I feel very good about him, I’m very optimistic, I don’t think Texans are going to vote for a criminal, cheat, adulterer, Ken Paxton," she said. When I pointed out that Paxton, the current state attorney general, had already won statewide elections twice, she smiled and said, "That’s the problem." But not the only problem. Asked about Talarico’s Senate primary opponent, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, a high-profile Black Texas Democrat who has thus far refused to back Talarico, Ellen said, "I voted for her, and after he won…and she decided she wasn’t going to support him, I was so glad that she lost. JASMINE CROCKETT BLASTS HER TEXAS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY LOSS AS ‘RACIST RACE' Joanna and Ruth, who are in Ellen's age demo and also very active in the Democratic Party in Dallas, thought Talarico is looking good. ,"I’m feeling more encouraged than I have in a really long time, that it is going to flip over," Joanna added, "I’m feeling really fabulous about it too," but again, concerns over Crockett and the Black vote lingered. Joanna shared that, "I really hope she gets on board to help with the Black people, because we need them voting, but she has always been my rep and I love her." Several Black Democrats I spoke with at the event felt confident that Crockett’s obstinance would not be decisive, and were not willing to attack her for it. Perhaps the biggest headwind for Talarico that I discovered in Dallas, something that polling has a hard time catching up to, is a lack of enthusiasm over him. Determination to win is in the air, but far less so is excitement. Later that day, downtown, I met Richard who is in his 30s and works in the service industry. He said there was more buzz in the lead-up to Beto O’Rourke’s narrow 2018 Senate loss, "The energy for Beto was everywhere, it was palpable," he said. "I was sure that Ted Cruz was going to lose. I don’t feel that this time." Jaime, a liberal elementary school principal, seemed a bit less worried about the energy gap, though he did acknowledge, "Beto had style and rizz, Talarico is kind of a square." And let’s face it, back in 2018, we even had a term for O’Rourke’s appeal: ‘Beto-Mania.' There is no Talarico-Mania. I wound up asking several people this question, and even those who shrugged it off only did so after a look in their eyes told me they knew it was at least a real thing, if not a dealbreaker. Meanwhile, the massive on-hand money advantage that Talarico has enjoyed is starting to evaporate, as President Trump’s PAC this week committed $10 million to back Paxton. Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s ads, focused on oil production and culture issues, also serve as de facto anti-Talarico spots. On final bump in the road for Talarico is that in Texas, even among many Democrats, immigration is a tricky issue. Unlike in places like Michigan and Virginia, Democrats in Dallas were not saying they want to abolish ICE, but rather reform it. They do not want a return to Joe Biden’s policies on the southern border. Well do they recall the 15,000 Haitians lined up at the border in Del Rio, under Grandpa Joe’s watch. Curiously, a name that did not come up very often in my discussions with Democratic voters was Donald Trump, and after a decade of hearing little else from them, that was a bit jarring. REPUBLICAN PARTY TO HOST HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION IN DALLAS, TRUMP ANNOUNCES ON TRUTH SOCIAL Voters on the Left are realizing that they can’t simply run against Trump anymore, because The Donald is in the home stretch of his presidency. Time will succeed, where their party failed, in ending Trump’s tenure in the White House. The real question is, what comes next? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Will Texas be fool's gold for the Democrats again this year, as it has so often been, or will the new demography of blue state transplants finally get them over the top? For now, as Republicans are set to make their pitch in Dallas this week, the feeling is more one of worry than outright confidence. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DAVID MARCUS

articles.title: Who won’t be at RNC’s midterm convention in Dallas
articles.summary: Republicans are holding a midterm convention on Wednesday and Thursday in Dallas, two months out from a general election that will have high stakes for President Trump and his party. However, the convention comes at a rough political time for Republicans, with Trump’s approval rating slumping, the unpopular war in Iran recently stretching past the…
articles.body:
Republicans are holding a midterm convention on Wednesday and Thursday in Dallas, two months out from a general election that will have high stakes for President Trump and his party.

However, the convention comes at a rough political time for Republicans, with Trump’s approval rating slumping, the unpopular war in Iran recently stretching past the six-month mark and Democrats up in recent polling against Republicans on the generic ballot.

The convention, which has been branded as a “Trump-a-palooza,” has sparked mixed feelings among Republicans. Some have pointed to concerns about costs, timing and the possible political risk of being closely linked to Trump shortly before the election.

With those factors in the background, some Republicans are avoiding the convention altogether. Here’s what you need to know about the members of the GOP who are skipping out on the president’s “palooza.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is one of the more prominent figures who has decided not to go to the convention, as she faces a tough reelection battle. The Portland Press Herald reported that a spokesperson for the Maine senator said Collins “runs her own campaign independent of any national party schedule.”

Beyond Collins, Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said his time is better spent having constituent meetings in his home state and that he won’t go to Dallas.

“I’m back in the state of South Dakota,” Rounds, who is dealing with a race that is more challenging than usual, said after being questioned about the convention.

The South Dakota senator added, “That’s up to the folks that want to be there,” when asked if the midterm convention is a good idea.

Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) is also reportedly not taking part in the “Trump-a-palooza,” as he faces a challenge from former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska.).

On the other side of the coin, however, there are some Republicans aiming for a seat in the upper chamber that will be in Dallas this week.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Michael Whatley, Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), all dealing with challenging Senate elections this year, are scheduled to speak at the convention Wednesday night.

And Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who is facing more competition in his reelection race than expected, will also be in Dallas.

“We’re taking nothing for granted,” Marshall said. “We need the president’s base to get out and vote.”

House members staying home (or elsewhere)

Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar (Fla.), Tom Barrett (Mich.), Juan Ciscomani (Ariz.), Zach Nunn (Iowa) and David Valadao (Calif.) have decided against attending the convention, according to CNN . All but Salazar in that group are considered to be in “toss up” races by political handicapper Cook Political Report.

However, some other Republicans in the “toss up” and “lean R” categories are attending the convention, including Reps. Derrick Van Orden (Wis.) Rob Bresnahan (Pa.), Monica De La Cruz (Texas), Ryan Mackenzie (Pa.) and Mike Lawler (N.Y.).

In a post on the social platform X on Tuesday, De La Cruz said that she would “be addressing the midterm convention in Dallas tomorrow.”

“Only in America can the granddaughter of a campesino who knelt in our fields, stand before a national audience like this. South Texas is a hardworking community, and I’m taking your message with me. Tune in!”
